name: Patrolling

origin.note: Boundary patrolling by agents with distinct speeds (ESA 2011).

summary: Robots move forever so that no point of a fence (a segment, a circle, or the edges of a graph) stays unvisited for long.
statement: $k$ robots with maximum speeds $v_1,\dots,v_k$ move forever along a **fence**: a segment, a circle, or the edges of a graph. The **idle time** is the largest time interval during which some point is not visited. The aim is to minimise it, or, equivalently, to find the longest fence that can be patrolled with idle time 1.

primer.intro: Security guards with different walking speeds must watch a long straight fence so that no point is left unvisited for too long. In fence patrolling the guards are $k$ **robots** with maximum speeds $v_1, \dots, v_k$ that move forever along the **fence**, here a segment; a point is **visited** when some robot is at it. The **idle time** is the longest stretch of time during which some point of the fence is not visited by any robot. Equivalently, fixing the idle time to 1, we ask for the longest fence, of length $\ell$, that the robots can patrol. Robots may pass each other, and the **schedule**, the motion of every robot over time, is planned in advance.

ideas.title: Partition: give each robot its own piece
ideas.idea:
The **partition** strategy:
1. Cut the fence into $k$ **pieces**, piece $i$ of length $v_i/2$.
2. Robot $i$ walks back and forth over its own piece at full speed, forever.
ideas.analysis: A round trip over piece $i$ takes $2 \cdot (v_i/2)/v_i = 1$, so every point of the piece is visited at least once in every unit of time, and the fence has length $\ell = (v_1 + \dots + v_k)/2$. On the other hand, in any unit of time robot $i$ visits a stretch of at most $v_i$, so no schedule patrols more than $v_1 + \dots + v_k$: partition is within a factor 2 of optimal. [Czyzowicz2011Patrolling] proved it optimal for $k = 2$ and conjectured it optimal for all $k$; [Kawamura2015Fence] confirmed $k = 3$.
ideas.why_it_matters: Partition is the natural first answer, and it is used as a building block in most patrolling strategies.

ideas.title: Every point needs $f+1$ visitors: a counting bound
ideas.idea: Now patrol a **graph**: **nodes** joined by **edges**, where each edge is a segment with a length; the fence is the union of the edges, of total length $|E|$. There are $k$ robots of speed 1, of which up to $f$ are **unreliable**: their visits do not count, and the **adversary**, an opponent who knows the schedule, picks them. Take any **window**, an interval of time of length $T$ equal to the idle time. If some point is visited in that window by only $f$ distinct robots or fewer, the adversary declares those robots unreliable and the point counts as not visited. So every point must be visited by at least $f+1$ different robots in the window.
ideas.analysis: Together the robots walk at most $kT$ in the window, and they must cover every point of every edge $f+1$ times, which needs at least $(f+1)|E|$. Hence $T \ge (f+1)|E|/k$. [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen] match it on graphs where a **closed walk** (a route along edges that ends where it starts) uses every edge exactly once: spread the robots evenly along that walk, $|E|/k$ apart, so every point is visited by a new robot every $|E|/k$ time units; in general they use a shortest closed walk through all edges and show that finding the optimum is NP-hard.
ideas.why_it_matters: Counting total work against what must be covered is the simplest lower-bound technique in patrolling, and it is tight here.

ideas.title: Six robots beat the partition
ideas.idea:
Take six robots with speeds $1, 1, 1, 1, 7/3, 1/2$. Partition patrols a fence of length $(1+1+1+1+7/3+1/2)/2 = 41/12$. [Kawamura2015Fence] patrol a longer fence, of length $7/2$:
1. The four robots of speed 1 walk end to end, covering most of the fence in a staggered pattern.
2. The fast robot covers most of what they leave uncovered.
3. The slowest robot fills the last small gaps.
ideas.analysis: Since $7/2 = 42/12 > 41/12$, the conjecture that partition is always optimal is false; adding further robots shows it fails for every $k \ge 6$. Later schedules patrol fences up to $4/3$ times longer than partition [Kawamura2020Simple], and on a circle simple strategies can be beaten by a factor $21/20$. The optimal schedule for general speeds is unknown.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that sharing pieces of the fence can beat dividing it, which is why even this one-dimensional problem is still open.

glossary.definition: a point that moves along the fence, robot $i$ at speed at most $v_i$; robots may pass each other
the set of points to be patrolled: a segment of length $\ell$, a circle, or the union of the edges of a graph
a point is visited at time $t$ when some robot is at that point at time $t$
the largest length of a time interval during which some point of the fence is not visited by any (reliable) robot
the motion of every robot over all time, fixed in advance
the strategy that cuts the fence into $k$ pieces, piece $i$ of length $v_i/2$, and lets robot $i$ walk back and forth over piece $i$ at full speed
a segment of the fence assigned to one robot by the partition strategy
a set of nodes joined by edges, each edge a segment with a length; patrolling a graph means patrolling every point of every edge
an endpoint of edges of the graph
a segment of the graph between two nodes; $|E|$ denotes the total length of the edges
a route along edges of the graph that ends at the node where it starts
said of one of the at most $f$ robots, chosen by the adversary, whose visits do not count
an interval of time whose length $T$ equals the idle time
an opponent that knows the schedule and chooses which robots are unreliable

history: Patrolling asked first for **optimal strategies** and whether the simple ones, partitioning the fence or cycling around it, are optimal [Czyzowicz2011Patrolling]. They are not in general [Kawamura2015Fence] [Kawamura2020Simple]; faults later changed the question to the idle time a graph admits when up to $f$ patrollers are unreliable [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen].

measures.name: Idle time
measures.description: worst idle time, or the longest fence patrollable with idle time 1 (stated per variant)

axes.name: Fence

values.label: the edges of a graph
values.definition: Every point of every edge of a graph $G$ must be visited; robots move along edges.

values.label: a segment (open fence)
values.definition: An open fence: the segment $[0,\ell]$; robots may reverse direction anywhere.

values.label: a circle (closed fence)
values.definition: A closed fence: a circle of length $\ell$.

axes.origin: Patrolling asks agents to visit every point of a terrain often enough; the measure is the idle time, the longest time a point is left unvisited [Kawamura2015Fence]. Czyzowicz, Gąsieniec, Kosowski and Kranakis proposed the open fence (a segment) and the closed fence (a circle) for agents with distinct speeds at ESA 2011, and conjectured that simple strategies are optimal on both [Czyzowicz2011Patrolling] (as reported by [Kawamura2020Simple]). Kawamura and Kobayashi disproved the segment conjecture [Kawamura2015Fence], and Kawamura and Soejima showed that optimal schedules can beat the simple strategies by factors $4/3$ on the segment and $21/20$ on the circle [Kawamura2020Simple]. They note that "finding an optimal strategy is not at all straightforward, even when the terrain is as simple as it could be" [Kawamura2020Simple]. Graphs, the most general domain, were studied by Czyzowicz et al. with unreliable robots: the domain is "represented by all points belonging to the graph edges", and edges are rectifiable curves whose lengths are their weights [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen].

variants.title: Open fence, distinct speeds
variants.summary: Partitioning the segment among the agents is optimal for 2 and 3 agents but not in general; optimal schedules can be up to $4/3$ better.

results.note: Introduces patrolling by agents with distinct speeds; shows the partition strategy optimal for $k=2$ and conjectures it optimal for every $k$, as stated by [Kawamura2015Fence], who disproved the conjecture.
Schedules that patrol a segment $4/3$ times longer than partition.

time.note: The best ratio between optimal schedules and partition is not known.

open: How much better than partition can an optimal schedule be on a segment, and is the problem of computing an optimal schedule hard?

variants.title: Closed fence, distinct speeds
variants.summary: On a circle, optimal schedules can beat the simple strategies by a factor $21/20$.

variants.title: Graphs with faulty patrollers
variants.summary: With at most $f$ unreliable robots among $k$, the optimal idle time lies between $(f+1)|E|/k$ and $(f+1)\,\mathrm{CPT}(G)/k$, which coincide on Eulerian graphs; computing it is NP-hard.

preconditions: every point must be passed by at least $f+1$ robots within each idle window, else the adversary makes them all faulty

lower_bounds.note: Theorem 4: deciding whether the idle time equals $\tfrac23|E|$ is NP-hard.

results.note: Introductory and current best: robots equally spaced along a Chinese Postman Tour (Theorem 3); equals $(f+1)|E|/k$ on Eulerian graphs (Corollary 1). For a segment with $f < k/2 - 1$ the paper gives a three-group strategy that is optimal for odd $f$ and almost optimal for even $f$ (Theorems 1 and 2).

time.note: Exact on Eulerian graphs; within a factor $\mathrm{CPT}(G)/|E| \le 2$ in general.

open: Is the decision version of fault-tolerant patrolling in NP? With $k$ part of the input and integer edge lengths it is in PSPACE [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen].
Optimal fault-tolerant patrolling of a segment when $f \ge k/2 - 1$, and for even $f$ [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen].
Approximation algorithms for the optimal idle time on general graphs [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen].
variants.notes: Faulty here means a robot whose visits do not count; the adversary chooses the faulty set knowing the strategy. $\mathrm{CPT}(G)$ is the length of a Chinese Postman Tour of $G$. Kotzig graphs (cubic graphs whose three perfect matchings pairwise form Hamiltonian cycles) attain the minimum idle time $\tfrac23|E|$, the number of their vertices, for $k = 3$, $f = 1$ (Corollary 2). The problem was posed at a MITACS workshop in 2012. Checked against the full text of [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen].
variants.statement: $k$ unit-speed robots move perpetually along the edges of a connected graph $G$ whose edges are curves of given lengths; $|E|$ is the total length. Knowing the strategy, an adversary chooses a set of $f$ faulty robots, whose visits do not count, a point $p$ and a time $t$. The idle time of a strategy is the supremum, over these choices, of the length of an interval starting at $t$ during which no reliable robot visits $p$; the goal is to minimise it.

figure.caption: Fence patrolling: robots with maximum speeds $v_1, \dots, v_k$ move forever along a segment so as to minimise the idle time, the longest interval during which some point is not visited. The animation runs the partition strategy [Czyzowicz2011Patrolling] with speeds $1, 2, 1$: robot $i$ sweeps its own piece, of length $v_i/2$, back and forth at full speed (bars: the part swept on the way out, then on the way back), so every point is visited again within time 1 and a fence of length $(v_1 + \dots + v_k)/2$ is patrolled; this is not always optimal [Kawamura2015Fence].

frames.label: Time 1/2: each robot turns at the end of its piece
Final: back after time 1; every point visited again
